academic_standards_framework.AS1: Conceptual Understanding (Explaining historical events, geographic phenomena, political systems, economic concepts)
academic_standards_framework.AS2: Reading the text (given), understanding and interpretation (Analyzing given excerpts, source boxes, speeches)
academic_standards_framework.AS3: Information Skills (Bar graphs, pie charts, tables, timelines, data collection and analysis)
academic_standards_framework.AS4: Reflection on contemporary issues and questioning (Expressing opinions on current problems, environmental threats, democratic rights)
academic_standards_framework.AS5: Mapping Skills (Locating places on outline map of India / World, drawing sketches, reading map keys)
academic_standards_framework.AS6: Appreciation and Sensitivity (Appreciating cultural diversity, constitutional values, freedom fighters, empathy toward marginalized)

history.title_en: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
core_themes: Frédéric Sorrieu's utopian vision (1848 print)
The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation (Civil Code of 1804 / Napoleonic Code)
The Making of Nationalism in Europe (Aristocracy and the new middle class, Liberal nationalism, Zollverein 1834)
Conservatism after 1815 (Treaty of Vienna 1815)
The Revolutionaries: Giuseppe Mazzini, Young Italy, Young Europe
The Age of Revolutions: 1830–1848 (Greek War of Independence, Romanticism, Johann Gottfried Herder, Hunger, Hardship and Popular Revolt)
Unification of Germany (Otto von Bismarck, Blood and Iron, 1871 Kaiser William I)
Unification of Italy (Cavour, Garibaldi, Victor Emmanuel II 1861)
The Strange Case of Britain (Act of Union 1707, British flag Union Jack)
Visualising the Nation: Allegories (Marianne in France, Germania in Germany)
Nationalism and Imperialism: The Balkan Crisis (Powder keg of Europe leading to WWI)
First World War, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation
The Idea of Satyagraha (Champaran 1917, Kheda 1917, Ahmedabad 1918)
Rowlatt Act (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919 by General Dyer)
Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922): Nagpur Congress Session 1920, Chauri Chaura incident (1922)
Differing strands within the movement (Movement in Towns, Rebellion in the Countryside: Baba Ramchandra in Awadh, Tribal revolt: Alluri Sitarama Raju in Rampa hills of Andhra Pradesh)
Swaraj in the Plantations (Inland Emigration Act of 1859)
Towards Civil Disobedience: Simon Commission (1928), Lahore Congress (1929) and Purna Swaraj
The Salt March (Dandi March, 12 March to 6 April 1930) and Civil Disobedience Movement
How Participants saw the Movement (Rich peasants, Poor peasants, Business classes: FICCI, Industrial working class, Women)
Limits of Civil Disobedience: Untouchables (Dalits), Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, Poona Pact (September 1932), Muslim political organizations
The Sense of Collective Belonging (Bharat Mata painting by Abanindranath Tagore, Vande Mataram by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, folklore, tricolour flag)

history.title_en: The Making of a Global World
core_themes: Pre-modern world: Silk Routes linking Asia, Europe, and Northern Africa
Food travels: Spaghetti and potato; Conquest, disease (Smallpox) and trade in the Americas
The Nineteenth Century (1815–1914): Flow of trade, flow of labour, flow of capital
Corn Laws abolition and globalization of agriculture; Rinderpest (Cattle Plague) in Africa (1890s)
Indentured labour migration from India (Fiji, Caribbean, Mauritius, Trinidad: Hosay festival, Chutney music)
Indian entrepreneurs abroad: Shikaripuri shroffs, Nattukottai Chettiars
Inter-war Economy: Wartime transformations, Mass production (Henry Ford assembly line) and Great Depression (1929)
Post-war Settlement: Bretton Woods Institutions (IMF and World Bank), G-77 nations and NIEO
Proto-industrialisation in rural Europe
Coming up of the factory: James Watt steam engine, Richard Arkwright cotton mill
Hand labour vs Steam power; Life of workers in Victorian Britain (Luddism, Spinning Jenny attack)
Industrialisation in the Colonies: Age of Indian textiles, Decline of Surat and Hoogly, Rise of Bombay and Calcutta
What happened to weavers? The Gomasthas and conflicts with weavers
Manchester comes to India: Import tariffs, collapse of Indian weaving industry
Factories come up: First cotton mill in Bombay (1854), first jute mill in Bengal (1855)
Early entrepreneurs: Dwarkanath Tagore, Dinshaw Petit, Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata, Seth Hukumchand
Market for goods: Advertisements, labels (Made in Manchester), calendars, nationalist imagery

history.title_en: Print Culture and the Modern World
core_themes: The First Printed Books: China (Woodblock printing, accordion book), Japan (Diamond Sutra 868 AD), Korea
Print comes to Europe: Marco Polo brings woodblock printing from China to Italy (1295)
Johann Gutenberg and the Printing Press (Mainz, Germany 1430s; first printed book: Gutenberg Bible)
The Print Revolution and its Impact: Reading public, oral culture, religious debates and Protestant Reformation (Martin Luther 95 Theses 1517)
Print and the French Revolution: Enlightenment thinkers (Voltaire, Rousseau), mocking royalty
Nineteenth Century: Children, women, and workers as readers (Penny dreadfuls, lending libraries)
India and the World of Print: Manuscripts before print, Portuguese missionaries introduce print in Goa (mid-16th century)
Religious Reform and Public Debates: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Sambad Kaumudi), Samachar Chandrika, Deoband Seminary
New Forms of Publication: Novels, short stories, visual images (Raja Ravi Varma prints), caricatures
Women and Print: Rashsundari Debi (Amar Jiban), Tarabai Shinde (Stripurushtulna), Pandita Ramabai, Begum Rokeya
Print and the Poor: Jyotirao Phule (Gulamgiri 1873), B.R. Ambedkar, E.V. Ramasamy Periyar, Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
Print and Censorship: Vernacular Press Act (1878) modeled on Irish Press Laws, Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Kesari)

Classification of resources: Origin (Biotic/Abiotic), Exhaustibility (Renewable/Non-renewable), Ownership (Individual, Community, National, International), Status of development (Potential, Developed stock, Reserves)
Sustainable development: Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit 1992, Agenda 21
Resource planning in India: Identification and inventory, evolving planning structure, matching with national development plans
Land resources and Land use pattern in India: Net Sown Area, Forest cover (National Forest Policy 1952 target 33%)
Land degradation and conservation measures: Overgrazing (Gujarat, Rajasthan), Over-irrigation (Punjab, Haryana), Mining (Jharkhand, Odisha)
Soil as a Resource: Soil profile, Classification of soils in India (Alluvial, Black/Regur, Red and Yellow, Laterite, Arid, Forest/Mountain soils)
Soil erosion and conservation: Gully erosion, Sheet erosion, Wind erosion; Contour ploughing, Terrace farming, Strip cropping, Shelter belts
Flora and Fauna in India: Biodiversity, IUCN categories (Normal, Endangered, Vulnerable, Rare, Endemic, Extinct species)
Causes of depletion of flora and fauna: Colonial forestry, agricultural expansion, shifting cultivation (Jhum), mining, river valley projects
Conservation of forest and wildlife in India: Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Project Tiger (1973)
Types and distribution of forests: Reserved forests, Protected forests, Unclassed forests
Community and Conservation: Chipko Movement (Uttarakhand), Beej Bachao Andolan (Tehri), Joint Forest Management (JFM - Odisha 1988), Sacred Groves (Bhairondev Dakav 'Sonchuri')
Water scarcity and the need for water conservation and management
Multi-purpose river projects and integrated water resources management: 'Temples of modern India' (Jawaharlal Nehru)
Opposition to large dams: Displacement of local communities, environmental destruction (Narmada Bachao Andolan, Tehri Dam Andolan)

Rainwater Harvesting: Traditional systems (Guls/Kuls in Western Himalayas, Johads and Khadins in Rajasthan, Rooftop rainwater harvesting in Tamil Nadu - mandatory by law, Tankas in Bikaner/Phalodi, Bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya)
Types of farming: Primitive subsistence farming (Slash and burn / Jhumming), Intensive subsistence farming, Commercial farming (Plantations)

Cropping seasons in India: Rabi (Winter: wheat, barley, peas, gram, mustard), Kharif (Monsoon: paddy, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, cotton, jute, groundnut), Zaid (Summer: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables)
Major Crops of India: Food crops (Rice, Wheat, Millets: Jowar, Bajra, Ragi, Maize, Pulses), Food crops other than grains (Sugarcane, Oilseeds, Tea, Coffee: Arabica, Horticulture crops)
Non-food crops: Rubber, Fibre crops (Cotton - black soil, Jute - Golden fibre)

Technological and Institutional Reforms: Collectivization, Green Revolution, White Revolution (Operation Flood), Land development programmes, Kissan Credit Card (KCC), Minimum Support Price (MSP), Bhoodan-Gramdan movement (Vinoba Bhave)
map_points: Major areas of Rice and Wheat
Largest producers of Sugarcane (UP), Tea (Assam), Coffee (Karnataka), Rubber (Kerala), Cotton (Gujarat/Maharashtra), Jute (West Bengal)

core_themes: Mode of occurrence of minerals: Igneous/metamorphic rocks (veins/lodes), Sedimentary rocks (beds/layers), Residual mass of weathered material, Alluvial deposits (placer deposits), Ocean waters

Ferrous Minerals: Iron ore (Magnetite 70% Fe, Hematite 50-60% Fe; Major belts: Odisha-Jharkhand, Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur, Ballari-Chitradurga-Chikkamagaluru-Tumakuru, Maharashtra-Goa), Manganese (Odisha largest)
Non-Ferrous Minerals: Copper (Khetri in Rajasthan, Balaghat in MP, Singhbhum in Jharkhand), Bauxite (Odisha largest, Panchpatmali deposits)
Non-Metallic Minerals: Mica (Koderma-Gaya-Hazaribagh in Jharkhand, Nellore in AP, Ajmer in Rajasthan), Limestone
Conservation of Minerals
Energy Resources: Conventional (Coal: Anthracite, Bituminous, Lignite, Peat; Petroleum: Mumbai High, Ankaleshwar, Digboi; Natural gas: Krishna-Godavari basin; Electricity: Hydroelectric, Thermal)

Non-Conventional Energy Sources: Nuclear/Atomic (Uranium in Jharkhand/Aravalli, Monazite sand in Kerala), Solar energy, Wind power (Tamil Nadu Nagarcoil to Madurai, Jaisalmer), Biogas (Gobar gas), Tidal energy (Gulf of Khambhat/Kutch), Geothermal energy (Parvati valley HP, Puga valley Ladakh)
map_points: Iron Ore Mines: Mayurbhanj, Durg, Bailadila, Bellary, Kudremukh
Coal Mines: Raniganj, Bokaro, Talcher, Neyveli
Oil Fields: Digboi, Naharkatia, Mumbai High, Bassien, Kalol, Ankaleshwar
Nuclear Power Plants: Narora, Rawatbhata, Kakrapar, Tarapur, Kaiga, Kalpakkam

core_themes: Importance of manufacturing: Backbone of development, modernization of agriculture, eradicating poverty/unemployment, export earnings
Contribution of industry to national economy
Industrial location factors: Raw materials, labour, capital, power, market, agglomeration economies
Classification of industries: Agro-based vs Mineral-based; Key/Basic vs Consumer; Small-scale vs Large-scale; Public, Private, Joint, Cooperative sector
Agro-based Industries: Textile industry (Cotton, Jute: Hooghly river basin advantages, Sugar industry: shifting towards Southern/Western states)

Mineral-based Industries: Iron and Steel (Chota Nagpur plateau concentration, TISCO), Aluminium smelting, Chemical industries, Fertilizer industry (Nitrogenous/Urea, DAP), Cement industry, Automobile industry, Information Technology and Electronics (Bengaluru - Silicon Valley of India)
Industrial Pollution and Environmental Degradation: Air, Water, Thermal, Noise pollution; Control measures (Effluent treatment, rainwater harvesting, smoke precipitators)
Transport: Roadways (Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways, National Highways NH-44, State Highways, District Roads, Border Roads: BRO, Atal Tunnel), Advantages of roadways over railways
Railways: Principal mode of transportation for freight and passengers
Pipelines: Transporting crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas (HVJ pipeline)

Waterways: Inland waterways (NW-1 Ganga Allahabad to Haldia, NW-2 Brahmaputra, NW-3 West Coast Canal), Major Sea Ports (Kandla/Deendayal, Mumbai, JNPT, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam - deepest landlocked port, Paradip, Kolkata, Haldia)
Airways: Air India, Pawan Hans Helicopters; Communication: Personal communication, Mass communication (Doordarshan, AIR, Newspapers)
International Trade: Export and Import, Balance of Trade (Favourable vs Unfavourable), Tourism as a Trade
map_points: Major Sea Ports: Kandla, Mumbai, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi, Tuticorin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kolkata
International Airports: Amritsar (Raja Sansi), Delhi (Indira Gandhi), Mumbai (Chhatrapati Shivaji), Chennai (Meenambakkam), Kolkata (Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose), Hyderabad (Rajiv Gandhi)

core_themes: Case studies: Belgium (Flemish 59% Dutch, Wallonia 40% French, Brussels 80% French 20% Dutch) and Sri Lanka (Sinhala 74% Buddhist, Tamil 18% Hindu/Muslim)
Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka: 1956 Act making Sinhala sole official language, preferential policies, Sri Lankan Tamil alienation and civil war
Accommodation in Belgium: Constitutional amendments (1970–1993), equal Dutch and French ministers, community government, Brussels model as headquarters of European Union
Why power sharing is desirable? Prudential reasons (reduces possibility of conflict between social groups) vs Moral reasons (spirit of democracy)

Forms of power-sharing: Horizontal division (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary - Checks and balances), Vertical division (Federalism: Union, State, Local), Social groups (Reserved constituencies), Political parties, pressure groups and social movements (Coalition governments)

What is Federalism? Two or more tiers of government, jurisdictions demarcated by Constitution, fundamental provisions require consent of both levels, courts act as umpire, dual objective: safeguard unity and accommodate regional diversity
'Coming together' federations (USA, Switzerland, Australia) vs 'Holding together' federations (India, Spain, Belgium)

What makes India a federal country? Three-fold distribution of legislative powers: Union List (97 subjects: Defence, foreign affairs, banking, currency), State List (66 subjects: Police, trade, agriculture, irrigation), Concurrent List (47 subjects: Education, forest, trade unions, marriage; Union law prevails in conflict), Residuary subjects (Cyber law)
Special provisions: Article 371 for North-Eastern states, Union Territories

How is federalism practiced in India? Linguistic States (States Reorganization Commission 1956), Language Policy (No national language; Hindi official language with 21 other Scheduled Languages in 8th Schedule), Centre-State relations (Pre-1990 single party dominance vs Post-1990 Coalition era and Supreme Court ruling on Article 356)

Decentralisation in India: 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (1992): Mandatory regular elections, reservation for SC/ST/OBC, 1/3rd seats for women, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission
Rural Local Government (Panchayati Raj: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti / Mandal, Zilla Parishad) and Urban Local Government (Municipalities, Municipal Corporations - Mayor)
Gender and Politics: Sexual division of labour, Feminist movements, Patriarchal society
Women's political representation: Low percentage in Parliament/Assemblies, Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women's Reservation Act), 1/3rd seats in Panchayati Raj

Religion, Communalism and Politics: Communal politics (one religion presented as superior to others), Communal riots, Secular State provisions in Indian Constitution (Articles 25-28, no official religion)

Caste and Politics: Caste inequalities and caste hierarchy breakdown (urbanization, literacy, economic development), Caste in politics (appealing to caste vote banks), Politics in caste (backward/forward coalitions, Dalits and OBC assertion)
Why do we need political parties? Meaning, three components: leaders, active members, followers
Functions of political parties: Contest elections, put forward policies/programmes, making laws, form and run government, role of opposition, shape public opinion, access to government machinery
Party systems: One-party system (China), Two-party system (USA, UK), Multi-party system (India, coalition governments)
National Parties vs State Parties (Election Commission criteria): National Party (6% votes in Lok Sabha or Assembly in 4 states + 4 seats in Lok Sabha; e.g. BJP, INC, AAP, BSP, CPI-M)
Challenges to political parties: Lack of internal democracy, Dynastic succession, Money and muscle power, Lack of meaningful choice to voters
How can parties be reformed? Anti-defection law (52nd Amendment), Affidavit declaring assets/criminal cases, Election Commission order for organizational elections, State funding of elections

How do we assess democracy's outcomes? Promotes equality among citizens, enhances dignity of the individual, improves quality of decision making, provides method to resolve conflicts, allows room to correct mistakes
Accountable, responsive and legitimate government: Right to Information (RTI), transparency, regular free and fair elections
Economic growth and development: Comparison of democracies and dictatorships (economic growth slightly higher in dictatorships, but democracy preferred for reducing poverty and inequality)
Reduction of inequality and poverty
Accommodation of social diversity: Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion; majority must work with minority
Dignity and freedom of the citizens: Women's rights, caste discrimination elimination

What Development Promises: Different people, different goals (Landless rural labour vs Prosperous farmer vs Urban unemployed youth; Conflicting goals: Dam construction benefits industrialists but displaces tribals)
Income and other goals: Money/material goods vs Freedom, security, respect, equal treatment
National Development: Comparing different countries/states using Per Capita Income (Average Income = Total Income / Total Population)
World Bank classification (World Development Report): High income countries (PCI > $12,055) vs Low income countries (PCI < $1,035)
Income and other criteria: Comparison of Haryana, Kerala, and Bihar (Infant Mortality Rate IMR, Literacy Rate, Net Attendance Ratio)
Public Facilities: Why average income is inadequate (Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment or protect from infectious diseases), Public Distribution System (PDS)
Human Development Report (UNDP): Human Development Index (HDI) based on Life Expectancy, Educational attainment (mean years of schooling), Per Capita Gross National Income (GNI)
Sustainability of Development: Groundwater depletion in India, Exhaustion of natural crude oil reserves

Classification of Economic Activities: Primary Sector (Agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry), Secondary Sector (Manufacturing, industrial activity), Tertiary Sector (Services: transport, banking, trade, IT, communication)
Comparing the Three Sectors: Calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP = Value of all final goods and services produced in each sector in a financial year)
Historical Changes in Sectors: Primary to Secondary to Tertiary dominance in developed nations
Rising importance of the Tertiary Sector in India: Basic services (hospitals, schools, police), development of agriculture and industry, rise in income levels, new services (IT, telecom)
Where are most of the people employed? Share of sectors in GDP vs Employment (Tertiary generates max GDP, but Primary employs ~44% of workforce)
Underemployment / Disguised Unemployment: More people working than needed in agriculture
How to create more employment? Cheap agricultural credit, irrigation (wells, canals), rural transport and storage, agro-processing industries, rural tourism and education
MGNREGA 2005 (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act): 100 days of guaranteed wage employment, unemployment allowance if not provided

Division of sectors as Organised and Unorganised: Organised (Job security, fixed working hours, paid leave, provident fund, gratuity, Factories Act) vs Unorganised (Low wages, no job security, irregular employment, no benefits)

Sectors in terms of ownership: Public Sector (Government owns assets and provides services: Railways, Post office; purpose is social welfare) vs Private Sector (Ownership in hands of private individuals: TATA, Reliance; purpose is profit)
Money as a medium of exchange: Barter system and Double coincidence of wants
Modern forms of money: Currency (paper notes and coins, authorized by Government of India and RBI), Demand Deposits in banks (Cheque facility)
Loan activities of Banks: Banks keep ~15% of deposits as cash reserve, extend remaining as loans; Interest spread is main source of bank income
Two different credit situations: Festival season (Profitable credit - Salim shoe manufacturer) vs Crop failure (Debt trap - Swapna farmer)
Terms of Credit: Interest rate, Collateral (security asset), Documentation requirement, Mode of repayment
Formal Sector Credit in India: Commercial banks and Cooperatives (Supervised by RBI: maintains cash reserve ratio, lends to small borrowers and farmers, low interest rates)
Informal Sector Credit: Moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives (No supervision, exorbitant interest rates, debt traps)
Self-Help Groups (SHGs) for the poor: 15–20 members (especially women), pooling small savings, low-interest internal loans, bank linkage without collateral, empowerment of rural women
Production across countries: Multinational Corporations (MNCs) spreading production globally for lowest cost and proximity to markets

Interlinking production across countries: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), partnerships with local companies, acquiring local companies (Cargill Foods buying Parakh Foods), placing orders with small producers (garments, footwear)
Foreign trade and integration of markets: Producers sell beyond domestic borders; Chinese toys in India case study
What is Globalisation? Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through movement of goods, services, investments, and technology

Factors enabling globalisation: Technology (Container transport, Information and Communication Technology - ICT, Internet), Liberalisation of foreign trade and investment policy (Removal of trade barriers like tariffs and import quotas in 1991 New Economic Policy)
World Trade Organisation (WTO): Established 1995, Geneva, promotes free trade, debate on agricultural subsidies in developed nations

Impact of Globalisation in India: Benefits for urban consumers (wider choice, superior quality, lower prices), Top Indian companies become MNCs (Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints), Creation of jobs in IT/services (call centres, software)
Challenges for small producers: Competition, loss of livelihood (batteries, plastics, toys, dairy)
The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation: Role of government in protecting small producers, labour laws implementation, negotiating with WTO
The Consumer in the Marketplace: Unfair trade practices (adulteration, underweight, misleading advertisements)
Consumer Movement in India: Origins as a social force against food shortages, hoarding, black marketing

COPRA (Consumer Protection Act 1986) and Consumer Protection Act 2019: Establishment of three-tier quasi-judicial machinery (District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission up to ₹1 crore, State Commission ₹1 crore to ₹10 crore, National Commission above ₹10 crore)
Consumer Rights: Right to Safety, Right to be Informed (RTI Act 2005, MRP, expiry date, ingredients), Right to Choose, Right to be Heard, Right to Seek Redressal, Right to Consumer Education
Standardisation Marks: ISI mark (Industrial/electrical goods), AGMARK (Agricultural products), Hallmark (Gold jewellery), ISO certification
Consumer Awareness: National Consumer Day (24 December), 'Jago Grahak Jago' campaign
